title: £500 in a card
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on an elderly care ward. Mrs Abbott, 84, who you looked after for three weeks, was discharged home yesterday. Today a nurse hands you a card she left for you.

Inside is £500 in cash and a note: "For you personally. Thank you for being so kind."
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Keep the money and declare it on the gifts register.
options.brief: Declaring doesn't make a large cash gift acceptable.
options.detailed: Declaring is the right process for small gifts, but £500 in cash from an older patient who may be vulnerable shouldn't be kept.

options.text: Suggest to Mrs Abbott that the money goes to the ward charity, if she wishes.
options.brief: An alternative, if she wants to give something.
options.detailed: She may prefer this to having it returned. It ranks third because it should be offered as a choice, without pressure, after she has been told you can't keep it.

options.text: Contact Mrs Abbott to thank her and explain you can't accept the money.
options.brief: Kind, and makes sure she understands why it is coming back.
options.detailed: She deserves a warm thank-you, and an explanation so that the money's return doesn't feel like a rejection. It ranks second because the cash should be in the trust's process first, and the ward manager may want to coordinate the contact.

options.text: Keep the money, as it was a personal gift.
options.detailed: This could be seen as exploiting a vulnerable patient's gratitude. It is the least appropriate option.

options.text: Hand the card to the ward manager and follow the trust's gifts policy.
options.brief: Cash should be handled openly, through the trust's process.
options.detailed: A large cash gift needs to be recorded and kept safely, and the trust will have a process for returning it. Involving the ward manager straight away means the money is handled transparently, not by you alone. It ranks first.

explanation.issue: This tests how you handle a large cash gift from an older patient, transparently and kindly.
explanation.keyDetails: The gift is £500 in cash. She is 84 and may be vulnerable. The gift is personal. She has already gone home.
explanation.reasoning: [E] puts the money into the trust's process, [C] thanks her and explains, and [B] offers an alternative. [A] keeps an inappropriate gift, and [D] keeps it undeclared.
explanation.competing: Some would contact Mrs Abbott first, as a personal thank-you matters. The key hands the cash to the ward manager first, because money shouldn't be held informally, and the thank-you can follow the same day. If there were any sign she was being financially exploited, the ward manager could also raise it.

references.title: Identifying and managing conflicts of interest
references.note: Gifts from patients and the risk of appearing to influence care.
